newsitem.title: USA: Fed's Rivlin says economy doing fine.
newsitem.headline: Fed's Rivlin says economy doing fine.

text.p: The Federal Reserve's No. 2 policy-maker said Tuesday the economy may be doing better than ever but that the central bank was still watching to ensure growth did not become too much of a good thing.
"The American economy is doing fine," Fed Vice Chairwoman Alice Rivlin said. "It is as good a set of economic statistics at the aggregate level as American economists have seen, perhaps ever."
Rivlin was referring to the recent stream of data pointing to moderate economic growth, after a burst of growth in the fourth quarter, and tame inflation.

She also said that the tight job market -- the unemployment rate of 5.4 percent is near its lowest level in six years -- was not as worrisome as some economists have feared since it helps provide jobs to thousands of people who might otherwise be unemployed.

"Tight labour markets are basically a very good thing, not just for those looking for jobs now, but for the future health and productivity of our economy," she said in a speech to the Credit Union National Association, a trade group for credit unions.
She also made clear that the central bank was watching for signs of trouble that might turn the best of times into something worse.
She said the biggest potential threat was "too much of good thing, an overheated economy followed by inflation, a boom followed by a bust."
Rivlin's generally upbeat remarks came just a day before Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan goes to Capitol Hill to present his eagerly awaited semi-annual report on the economy to Congress.

Greenspan, in testimony before the Senate Banking Committee on Wednesday, is expected to echo Rivlin's general tone, arguing the economy is stable with remarkably low inflation as the expansion approaches its sixth birthday.

As always, Greenspan is also expected to say the Fed will continue to guard against price pressures that could lead to inflation. Some economists have worried that the tight job market could force companies to bid up wages and then raise prices.

Rivlin, in her remarks, said the tight labour market means people who might have been unemployed or on welfare in less vibrant times are getting critical job experience that will help them, and the economy, in the future.

"The best way to learn job skills is on the job," she said. "Tight labour markets mean that employers have incentives to use emplopees as effectively as they can, to offer training to move people to higher levels of responsibility sooner."
Rivlin contrasted this with Europe, where she said large numbers of young people were missing developing jobs skills and experience because of high unemployment rates.
"The tragedy of the prolonged high unemployment rate in France and Germany and other places is that so many people, especially young people, aren't learning any job skills," she said.
She also said the United States needed to invest more wisely in people to lift their skills and boost productivity.
"Our schools are not as good as they could be," she said.

Turning to the Fed's main enemy -- inflation -- Rivlin said she was gratified by prices in the United States, noting that businesses so far have been able to absorb wage increases without raising prices and profits have been holding up well.

"We can't be sure how long that will last, it's not likely that the ups and downs of the economy which we have known forever have suddenly gone away so the Federal Reserve is watching carefully, especially the price indices," she said.
Economists traditionally have said that an unemployment rate below 6 percent would lead to rising inflation. But the unemployment rate has been below 6 percent for 2-1/2 years.
